front.title: BGP best path next-hop selection enhancements

abstract.t: BGP [RFC4271] has originally been designed to carry IPv4 routing information over the Internet. IP routing being "hop-by-hop" in nature, NEXT_HOP which purpose is to carry the address of the next router to send the IP packet to. In BGP, the next-hop may not be a directly connected router, hence, when evaluating paths, a BGP speaker must determine if the next-hop is resolvable and, if so, determine the internal cost to reach it.

The incremental use of tunneling technologies to carry traffic between routers (e.g.: GRE, MPLS, SR-MPLS, SRv6...) may violate the assumption that the address carried in the NEXT_HOP is representative of the actual forwarding next-hop. These technologies decouple the BGP control-plane's view of the next-hop from the data-plane's actual forwarding endpoint. This document describes the problems that arise from this decoupling. These problems include sub-optimal path selection, incorrect resolvability tracking of the forwarding path leading to traffic drop or misrouting, and others. This document specifies how BGP uses path-resolution results and associated local policy as inputs to BGP path selection and how changes to those inputs are tracked.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: BGP is designed to exchange network reachability information between routing domains. A BGP update typically contains a prefix and a set of path attributes, including NEXT_HOP. The receiving router uses this next-hop address to determine the egress point for traffic destined for the advertised prefix. The underlying assumption is that the next-hop address represents the actual next router in the data plane's forwarding path.

Section 9.1.2.1 defines the route resolvability condition: a BGP route is considered unresolvable if the BGP speaker's routing table has no route matching the BGP route next-hop address. As per Section 9.1.2.2 e), when comparing paths received via internal BGP (IBGP), the metric to reach the BGP route's next-hop address, found in the routing table, is used to determine the best path.

In , RTR3 receives prefix P/m from RTR1 and RTR2 (IBGP peers) with NEXT_HOP N1 and N2. RTR3 resolves N1 with a cost of 1 and N2 with a cost of 2. Based on procedures, RTR3 will select the path with the lowest cost to the NEXT_HOP address, so RTR3 will select the path received from RTR1. In this example, the path used to resolve N1 and N2 reflects the actual forwarding path, which makes RTR3's best-path decision accurate.

This document describes cases where the NEXT_HOP used in the BGP update is not representative of the actual forwarding path. In these cases, the resolvability condition may fail in its goal and path selection may be done on inaccurate criteria leading to suboptimal routing, network congestion, traffic drop or misrouting...
These use cases are not new and may have been partially addressed by IETF standards or drafts, some references are provided below:

ul.li: addresses the case of MPLS networks and proposes a modification of the route resolvability condition to be performed using forwarding database of a particular data plane protocol. It also proposes an optional data path verification.

Section 7 improves the route resolvability condition by verifying that there is a feasible tunnel. However, it doesn't take into account that the cost associated with the tunnel may be different from the cost associated with the BGP next-hop.

defines SRv6 overlay services signaling using BGP. The procedures involve the advertisement of an SRv6 Service TLV within the BGP Prefix SID attribute to signal the SID to be used for forwarding. RFC9252 highlights that ingress PE must perform a resolvability check for the SRv6 SID in addition to the resolvability check done on the NEXT_HOP. However, it doesn't take into account that the cost associated with the SRv6 SID may be different from the cost associated with the BGP next-hop.

section.t: This document defines a common path-resolution model for these use cases. Each candidate path is associated with a path resolution tuple whose resolution provides inputs to BGP route selection. BGP uses these inputs to compare candidate paths and tracks resolution changes that may require the selection to be reevaluated.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.title: Unicast over a BGP-free core

figure.title: Next hop attribute not used for forwarding

section.t: In , an IPv4 unicast service is deployed over a BGP-free MPLS core. Let's assume PE3 receives prefix P/m from PE1 and PE2 with NEXT_HOP N1 and N2. The existence of a route in PE3's IPv4 routing table to reach N1 or N2 (defined in ) is not sufficient to ensure that traffic can be carried from PE3 to PE1 or PE2. PE3 needs to ensure that there is a tunnel available to reach PE1 or PE2 that can carry MPLS traffic (e.g.: an MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP)). By checking only for the existence of a route in its routing table, PE3 could create a traffic drop or misrouting if there is no tunnel to carry the IPv4 unicast traffic. This use case is also considered in .

section.title: Segment Routing Traffic Engineering Policy
section.t: When using SR Policies , the BGP NEXT_HOP may not accurately represent the actual forwarding path. When SR Policy candidate paths are distributed via BGP , the metric of their segment lists can be carried as specified in , allowing the SR Policy metric to be taken into account in the best-path selection.

In , a BGP VPN service (as defined in ) is deployed between the PEs. Let's assume PE3 receives prefix P/m from PE1 and PE2 with NEXT_HOP N1, N2 and color C1. On PE3, SR Policies (C1, N1) and (C1, N2) are configured to use the low latency path.

ul.li: Costs M in parentheses represents cost of IGP.
Costs D in brackets represents cost of latency-based metric

section.t: If PE3 performs next-hop resolution based solely on the BGP NEXT_HOP, it will not verify the existence and state of a corresponding SR Policy (C1, Nx). Consequently, it may select a suboptimal path by considering the cost to the NEXT_HOP address instead of the cost of the SR policy. The best path considering SR-policy (C1, Nx) cost is via PE2, while the best path considering IGP metric is via PE1.

Considering that PE3 may take into account the cost of the SR policy and then picks up the path from PE2 as best. If the SR Policy (C1, N2) is down or not present, and considering that color C1 uses Color-Only Type 0 (bits 00), as defined in Section 3, the steering procedures in Section 8.8.1 authorize the path from PE2 to use the IGP path to next-hop N2 (fallback to the IGP path via P1 with cost=6) when there is no policy (C1, N2) available. This situation has multiple drawbacks:

ul.li: The costs of the two BGP paths are not directly comparable, which makes the comparison inaccurate: the path via PE1 uses a latency-based cost, while the fallback path via PE2 uses an IGP metric.
Using a path without an SR-policy may violate the intent of the service, especially if there is an alternate path (from PE1) that fulfills the intent.

section.t: It may be desirable for PE3 to prefer the path from PE1 that satisfies color C1 or even exclude any path that does not meet the color C1 requirement.

section.title: SRv6 services
section.t: When using SRv6 services as defined in , the BGP NEXT_HOP may not be representative of the actual forwarding path.

Considering , an SRv6-based BGP VPN is deployed between the PEs. PE1 uses locator L1 for algorithm 0 and L1_FA for flexible algorithm 128 () optimized for low-latency. Similarly, PE2 uses locator L2 for algorithm 0 and L2_FA for flexible algorithm 128. Let's assume PE3 receives prefix P/m from PE1 and PE2 with NEXT_HOP N1, N2 and SRv6 SID S1 and S2. SID S1 and S2 are allocated respectively from L1_FA and L2_FA.

ul.li: Costs M in parentheses represents cost of algorithm 0 (as defined in Section 8.5).
Costs D in brackets represents cost of flexible algorithm 129 which is using low-latency metric.

section.t: The IPv6 routing table of PE3 contains the following entries:

Based on procedures, PE3 verifies that NEXT_HOP address of each path is resolvable. Based on procedures, PE3 verifies that S1 and S2 addresses are resolvable. PE3 will then select the path with the lowest cost to the NEXT_HOP address according to . Cost to N1 is lower than cost to N2, so PE3 will select the path received from PE1. However, from a latency perspective, path to PE2 is the best one.

The problem of path suboptimality may also happen with algorithm 0, if for instance SRv6 traffic for algorithm 0 needs to be offloaded from PE1, operator may increase the metric of the locator (while not changing the metric of the next-hop) on PE1. In the example above, if L1 is advertised by PE1 with an offset of 1M, then PE3 will have to cost to L1 of 1000002 but N1 will still be reachable with a cost of 2. The cost to reach the SID must also be taken into account in this scenario to ensure that the traffic offload works properly.

section.title: Path Resolution Inputs to BGP Route Selection
Path resolution tuple
section.t: This document defines a path resolution tuple as a resolution key and, when required, a resolution context. The resolution key identifies the object to be resolved for a BGP path. For the mechanisms defined in this document, the resolution key is an IP address. It may be the BGP NEXT_HOP or a different address signaled with the path, such as a Tunnel Egress Endpoint or an SRv6 Service SID.
The following data already defined in BGP standards SHOULD be considered as resolution keys:

ul.li: The Tunnel Egress Endpoint Sub-TLV contained in Tunnel Encapsulation attribute defined in
SRv6 SID Information Sub-TLV contained within L3 or L2 SRv6 SID defined in

section.t: Unless a BGP update contains another type of resolution key, the BGP NEXT_HOP is considered as the resolution key.

The resolution key MAY be complemented by a resolution context. When present, the resolution context identifies or parameterizes the resolution procedure and datastore used to resolve the resolution key. The following attributes defined in BGP standards are examples of resolution contexts:

ul.li: The Tunnel Encapsulation attribute defined in
The Color extended community defined in
The SRv6 Sub-TLV and Sub-sub-TLV contained within L3 or L2 SRv6 SID TLV as defined in other than the SID itself

section.t: Two path resolution tuples containing the same resolution key but differing in resolution context, including whether a context is present, are distinct resolution requests. For example, in the SR Policy use case above, {N1, C1} requests resolution through SR Policy (C1, N1), whereas {N1} requests resolution of next hop N1 without a route-carried resolution context.

Each new BGP extension SHOULD specify whether an address carried by the extension is a resolution key and, when applicable, how its resolution context is derived. The procedures defined in the next section SHOULD apply for any new resolution key without having to redefine them.

section.title: Resolution constraints
section.t: When a path resolution tuple is identified for a BGP route, the resolver uses the resolution key together with its resolution context, when present. Resolution constraints are rules applied when resolving a path resolution tuple. They restrict which routes or datastores may provide a valid resolution. These constraints are not additional components of the path resolution tuple and may be derived from the resolution context or configured locally.

In some cases, an operator may want to enforce that the resolution key is resolved through a specific type of route. This can be achieved by configuring a local resolution constraint. Reusing the example defined in , if we consider an IPv4 unicast BGP service carried over a BGP free-core, the BGP NEXT_HOP must be reachable through a tunnel to allow the end-to-end packet delivery. Such a case cannot be derived from the BGP update context and BGP must be configured to resolve the NEXT_HOP only through tunnels (of any or specific types). Similarly, when aggregate routes are present in the routing table, a user may want to prevent a resolution key that identifies a more-specific destination from being resolved over an aggregate route. A resolution constraint based on prefix/mask can be used to prevent such a resolution from being considered valid. An implementation MAY provide a set of configuration options for resolution constraints.

Another example of a resolution constraint is the "Resolution Scheme", defined in BGP Classful Transport . The "Resolution Scheme" constrains the resolution of the NEXT_HOP to an ordered set of transport classes dictated by the intent (Mapping Community) attached to the route.

section.title: Path-resolution result and preference

dl.dd: The outcome of resolving a path resolution tuple subject to the applicable resolution constraints. It indicates whether resolution succeeded. When resolution succeeds, the result identifies the resolution actually selected, including any fallback, and provides any available metric, forwarding information, and information needed to track changes. Each successful result used by the replacement route-selection procedure defined below is associated with a path-resolution preference.

A locally significant value that orders the resolution outcomes represented by path-resolution results. For any two preference values used in the same comparison, either the values are identical or the locally defined ordering MUST identify exactly one value as preferred to the other. The ordering MUST be consistent: if preference A is preferred to preference B and preference B is preferred to preference C, preference A MUST be preferred to preference C. The representation of a path-resolution preference and the source of its ordering are implementation matters. An implementation can derive the value from properties of the result or from local policy and can represent it numerically. This document does not require a numeric representation and does not specify whether a lower or a higher numeric value is more preferred. A path-resolution preference is not a BGP path attribute and is not advertised.

section.t: When the replacement route-selection procedure defined below is enabled, each path-resolution result under consideration for the same destination MUST be assigned a path-resolution preference from the same local ordering. Metrics provided by results assigned the same path-resolution preference MUST have common comparison semantics and use the same ordering. Results whose metrics cannot be meaningfully compared MUST be assigned different path-resolution preferences. For any two metrics provided by results assigned the same preference, the comparison MUST return exactly one of the following outcomes: the first metric is preferred, the second metric is preferred, or the metrics are equivalent. The comparison MUST be consistent: if metric A is preferred to metric B and metric B is preferred to metric C, metric A MUST be preferred to metric C; if metric A is equivalent to metric B and metric B is equivalent to metric C, metric A MUST be equivalent to metric C.

The path-resolution preference used for comparison MUST be associated with the resolution actually selected, including any fallback resolution. For example, when an intent-aware resolution falls back to best-effort transport, the applicable preference is the one associated with the selected best-effort result, not with the requested intent. The resolvability, selected resolution, path-resolution preference, metric, forwarding information, and tracking information used for a BGP path MUST all pertain to the same path-resolution result. An implementation MUST NOT combine inputs associated with different path-resolution results as if they described the same resolution.

section.title: Route resolvability condition
section.t: This document updates Section 9.1.2.1 as follows:

ul.li: The route resolvability check for the BGP NEXT_HOP MUST continue to be done.

The additional path resolution tuple resolvability check MAY be enabled through local configuration. When enabled, the path resolution tuple MUST be resolved subject to the applicable resolution constraints defined in . A route whose path resolution tuple cannot be resolved under those constraints MUST be treated as unresolvable.

section.title: Path-resolution preference and internal cost determination
section.t: For a prefix P/m, different BGP paths may use different path resolution tuples.

figure.artwork: P/m Path1: NH=10.0.0.1 Color: 200 Path2: NH=2001::2 SRv6-SID: cafe:0:2:e002:: Path3: NH=10.0.0.3 Tunnel-encap(L2TPv3, endpoint: 10.0.0.3) Path4: NH=2001::4 SRv6-SID: cafe:0:4:e002::

section.t: Metrics returned by different path-resolution results are not necessarily comparable because they can have different semantics or can be produced by different resolution procedures. For instance, Path1 can use an SR Policy that optimizes for latency, while Path2 can use an IGP metric and Path3 can have no metric. The numeric values associated with these results cannot be assumed to be comparable.

The need to distinguish metrics with different semantics is not new. A prefix can have BGP paths whose next hops are resolved by different IGPs or route types. Even when each resolution provides a numeric metric, comparing the values without common comparison semantics can produce an incorrect ordering.

When enabled, the following procedure replaces step e) of Section 9.1.2.2. For this procedure, the interior cost is obtained only from the path-resolution result. A metric obtained from the independently required BGP NEXT_HOP resolution MUST NOT be used as an additional or alternative interior cost.

When this replacement procedure is enabled, the additional path resolution tuple resolvability check defined in MUST also be enabled. A path whose path resolution tuple is unresolvable MUST be removed from consideration before it reaches this procedure.

ul.li: Retain only candidate paths whose path-resolution preference is the most preferred among the candidate paths.

Compare the metrics provided by the remaining path-resolution results using their common metric ordering. An absent metric MUST compare less preferred than every available metric and equivalent to another absent metric. Retain only paths whose metric is most preferred. Metrics that compare equivalently do not distinguish paths. If no remaining result provides a metric, skip the interior-cost comparison. This rule does not require an implementation to assign a numeric value to an absent metric.

section.t: To support controlled deployment and rollback, an implementation SHOULD provide local configuration to enable or disable the replacement procedure defined in this section. When the replacement procedure is disabled, the unmodified procedure in Section 9.1.2.2 e) applies.

The following example applies this procedure to the four paths shown above. Local policy assigns preference Tier-A to results that resolve through an SRv6 SID, Tier-B to results that resolve through an SR Policy, and Tier-C to results that resolve through L2TPv3. Tier-A is preferred to Tier-B, which is preferred to Tier-C. Metrics provided by the Tier-A results use the same IGP metric semantics and can be compared. The labels and their ordering are local to this example. An implementation can represent the ordering numerically, but such a representation has no protocol significance.

Path2 and Path4 have the most-preferred path-resolution preference, Tier-A, and are retained. Their metrics are comparable, and Path2 is selected because metric 12 is preferred to metric 14. Path1 and Path3 are not considered in the metric comparison because their path-resolution preferences are less preferred than Tier-A.

section.title: Next hop and path resolution tracking
section.t: For every path to which these procedures apply, a BGP speaker MUST maintain sufficient dependency information to detect changes in each applicable input: BGP NEXT_HOP resolvability; path resolution tuple resolvability or selected resolution; assigned path-resolution preference; and metric presence or value. Dependency tracking MUST distinguish path resolution tuples that have the same resolution key but different resolution contexts, including the absence of a resolution context.

A change to any dependency listed above MUST cause best-path selection to be re-evaluated for every destination having a path that depends on the affected BGP NEXT_HOP or path resolution tuple. Any change to local policy or configuration that alters the derivation or comparison of path-resolution results MUST cause best-path selection to be re-evaluated for every destination having a path to which the change applies. This includes changes to resolution constraints, resolution-selection or fallback policy, procedure enablement, preference assignment or ordering, metric ordering, or metric comparability.
These requirements apply to selected and non-selected paths.

section.title: Example
section.t: The example below illustrates how local policy orders path-resolution results before their metrics are compared. The preference names used in this example are illustrative and do not require any particular representation by an implementation.

In , a prefix P/m is reachable by PE4 through PE1, PE2, and PE3, with NEXT_HOP N1, N2, and N3, respectively. Because the network has a BGP-free core, traffic must be tunneled between edge devices. RSVP-TE provides traffic-engineered MPLS tunnels, while SR-MPLS provides best-effort reachability. PE4 uses a local resolution procedure that selects RSVP-TE when it is available and otherwise falls back to SR-MPLS. The RSVP-TE tunnel to PE3 cannot be established.

For BGP path comparison, PE4's local policy assigns the path-resolution preference Traffic-Engineered to results that select RSVP-TE and Best-Effort to results that select SR-MPLS. Traffic-Engineered is preferred to Best-Effort. The RSVP-TE metrics returned by results assigned Traffic-Engineered have common comparison semantics and can be compared. Metrics returned by Best-Effort results are not compared with RSVP-TE metrics because the results have different path-resolution preferences.
The IPv4 routing table below supports the independently required BGP NEXT_HOP resolvability check. Its metrics are not used as interior-cost inputs by the procedures in this document.

table.name: MPLS ingress tunnel table of PE4

section.t: As described in , PE4 applies a resolution constraint requiring the BGP NEXT_HOP to be resolved through an MPLS ingress tunnel. In this example, PE4 maintains the eligible tunnels in a separate datastore; this datastore organization is not required by the procedures in this document. N1 and N2 resolve through RSVP-TE, while N3 resolves through SR-MPLS because no RSVP-TE tunnel to PE3 is available. Resolution produces the following results, to which local policy assigns the shown path-resolution preference:

figure.artwork:
P/m Path1: from PE1, NH=N1 selected resolution: RSVP-TE tunnel to N1 path-resolution preference: Traffic-Engineered metric: 1000
Path2: from PE2, NH=N2 selected resolution: RSVP-TE tunnel to N2 path-resolution preference: Traffic-Engineered metric: 100
Path3: from PE3, NH=N3 selected resolution: SR-MPLS tunnel to N3 path-resolution preference: Best-Effort metric: 20

section.t: PE4 first applies the locally defined ordering of path-resolution preferences. Path3 is not considered further because its Best-Effort preference is less preferred than the Traffic-Engineered preference assigned to both Path1 and Path2. Path1 and Path2 have the same preference and their RSVP-TE metrics are comparable. PE4 selects Path2 because metric 100 is preferred to metric 1000 according to the local RSVP-TE metric ordering.

If the RSVP-TE tunnel to PE2 becomes unavailable, N2 remains resolvable through SR-MPLS, but its selected resolution changes from RSVP-TE to SR-MPLS and its path-resolution preference changes from Traffic-Engineered to Best-Effort. As described in , these changes cause PE4 to re-evaluate the affected paths, and Path1 becomes the best path. PE4 also re-evaluates the paths if a returned RSVP-TE metric changes; for example, Path1 becomes best if its metric becomes preferred to Path2's metric while both remain assigned Traffic-Engineered.

section.title: Example with Intent-Aware BGP Transport
section.t: This example illustrates how local policy can order path-resolution results when intent-aware BGP transport is deployed. Both BGP Classful Transport () and BGP Color-Aware Routing () can produce candidate paths that are resolved through different transport mechanisms whose metrics are not directly comparable. The preference names used below are illustrative local values.

In , PE3 receives a VPN prefix P/m from PE1 and PE2 with NEXT_HOP N1 and N2 respectively. An intent-aware transport technology is deployed, requesting "Gold" SLA transport for this prefix. Gold RSVP-TE tunnels exist from PE3 to PE1 but not from PE3 to PE2. Best-effort SR-MPLS tunnels exist to both PE1 and PE2.

In a BGP Classful Transport () deployment, P/m is advertised with Color Extended Community color:0:100 acting as a Mapping Community for the Gold transport intent. The Mapping Community maps the service route to a Resolution Scheme containing the ordered TRDB list [TRDB-Gold, TRDB-Best-Effort]. Following Section 7.8, the Resolution Scheme uses those TRDBs in order to resolve the BGP NEXT_HOP of each path:

ul.li: Path1 (NH=N1): a matching Tunnel Route for endpoint N1 is found in the primary TRDB, TRDB-Gold, and uses the RSVP-TE tunnel to PE1.
Path2 (NH=N2): no matching Tunnel Route for endpoint N2 is found in TRDB-Gold. A matching Tunnel Route is found in the backup TRDB, TRDB-Best-Effort, and uses the SR-MPLS tunnel to PE2.

section.t: In a BGP Color-Aware Routing () deployment, P/m is advertised as a service route carrying BGP Color Extended Community C_Gold. Following the service-steering procedures in Section 3, PE3 attempts to steer traffic for each service path over the corresponding color-aware path:

ul.li: Path1 (NH=N1): the color-aware path (N1, C_Gold), backed by RSVP-TE, is available and is selected.
Path2 (NH=N2): no color-aware path (N2, C_Gold) is available. Local service-steering policy permits fallback to a color-unaware best-effort path backed by SR-MPLS.

section.t: Although BGP Classful Transport resolution and BGP Color-Aware Routing service steering select different types of objects, their outcomes can be represented using the common path-resolution result model defined in this document. The selected object and resulting transport provide the available resolution and metric information; PE3's local policy assigns the path-resolution preference shown below.

In this example, local policy treats Gold as the requested transport property and best-effort as a permitted degraded fallback. It assigns the path-resolution preference Preferred-Transport to a result that selects Gold transport and Fallback-Transport to a result that selects best-effort fallback. Preferred-Transport is preferred to Fallback-Transport. This ordering is local: it does not require BGP to signal a preference value, mandate a numeric representation, or expose a routing-table preference.

If PE3 compared the returned metrics without considering their path-resolution results, it would compare 1000 with 15 and select Path2. That selection would use best-effort transport even though Path1 satisfies the requested Gold intent, and it would treat an RSVP-TE metric and an IGP metric as directly comparable.

PE3 instead applies its local path-resolution preference before comparing metrics. Because Preferred-Transport is preferred to Fallback-Transport, Path2 is not considered further and PE3 selects Path1. The metrics 1000 and 15 are not compared. If multiple candidate paths had the Preferred-Transport preference, local policy would be required to ensure that their metrics were meaningfully comparable before assigning that same preference.

figure.artwork:
P/m Path1: from PE1, NH=N1 resulting transport: Gold RSVP-TE path-resolution preference: Preferred-Transport metric: 1000
Path2: from PE2, NH=N2 resulting transport: best-effort SR-MPLS fallback path-resolution preference: Fallback-Transport metric: 15
=> PE3 selects Path1 because Preferred-Transport is preferred to Fallback-Transport

section.name: Operational Considerations
section.t: In most cases, tunnels carry traffic from the ingress to the egress node that advertised the BGP service route, as transit routers are not aware of the BGP service routes. For instance, in SRv6 service cases, the SRv6 encapsulation using the advertised SID as destination carries traffic down to the node that knows about the service route. Using the metric in the path-resolution result for the selected resolution as the internal cost makes sense in these cases because the selected resolution describes the end-to-end forwarding path.

However, there are cases where the tunnel does not terminate on the service egress. One example is a service route advertised with a color allowing for usage of a null endpoint policy. Another example is a service route advertised with a Tunnel Encapsulation attribute using a tunnel endpoint different from the service egress. In such cases, the tail node of the tunnel must have routing entries for the service routes to ensure end-to-end reachability.

In these cases, the metric in the path-resolution result for the selected resolution may not reflect the end-to-end path. The independently required NEXT_HOP resolution is not a second internal-cost input. Even if its metric were substituted, it would not necessarily provide a better view: it would still give an inaccurate picture of distances from a traffic forwarding perspective, since the forwarding path does not follow the IGP-routed path. Additionally, operators commonly manipulate the NEXT_HOP through routing policies, so there is no guarantee that the NEXT_HOP address correctly reflects the real egress node. Hence, the metric in the path-resolution result for the selected resolution when the tunnel tail is not the service egress is no less representative than such a hypothetical NEXT_HOP-derived metric.

This document specifies path-resolution inputs used by BGP route selection, including resolvability, path-resolution preference, and the metric associated with the selected result, when available. Consequently, the potential impact on routing loops needs to be analyzed.

The mechanisms described in this document are typically deployed in environments utilizing tunneling technologies (such as MPLS or SRv6). In these scenarios, BGP path selection determines the path resolution tuple whose resolution supplies the forwarding information used for encapsulation.

When the traffic is encapsulated at the ingress router, intermediate nodes forward packets based solely on the outer transport header rather than the inner destination. Consequently, the specific BGP selection criteria are enforced only at the ingress, preventing forwarding loops that might otherwise arise from inconsistent policy decisions on intermediate nodes.
To illustrate this loop prevention, consider the following topology where PE1, PE2, and PE3 provide reachability to Prefix X.

Assume PE1 is configured with the mechanisms defined in this document and selects PE2 as the BGP next-hop for Prefix X to optimize for low delay. Router P is a transit node and uses standard BGP procedures, preferring PE3 due to a lower IGP metric.

In a hop-by-hop IP routing paradigm, PE1 would forward a bare IP packet to P. Router P would perform a lookup on the inner destination IP (Prefix X) and deflect the packet toward PE3, directly contradicting PE1's decision and potentially causing a loop if PE3 also had a conflicting policy.

However, in a tunneling paradigm, PE1 encapsulates the packet with an outer header (e.g., an SRv6 SID or MPLS label) using forwarding information returned by resolution of the selected path's path resolution tuple. When the packet arrives at Router P, P only evaluates the outer header and forwards the packet along the IGP shortest path to PE2. Router P's BGP policy regarding Prefix X is never invoked for in-flight traffic.

Nevertheless, to ensure predictable routing behavior and simplify troubleshooting, it is recommended that network operators maintain consistent semantics for assigning and ordering path-resolution preferences and for comparing metrics between results assigned the same preference across all BGP speakers under the same administration. Because path-resolution preferences are locally significant, their internal representations need not be identical across speakers.

section.name: Relationship to draft-ietf-idr-bgp-bestpath-selection-criteria
section.t: This document and are complementary. Their relationship can be summarized as follows:

ul.li: Scope: performs the resolvability check only; this document also covers path-resolution preference, metric comparability, and internal cost determination.
Generality: is MPLS-centric; this document is generic and applies to MPLS, SR Policy, SRv6 and intent-aware BGP transport.
This document introduces the path resolution tuple, comprising a resolution key and an optional resolution context, while continuing to require BGP NEXT_HOP resolvability.

This document introduces path-resolution preference to order resolution results before the interior-cost comparison and requires any metrics provided by results assigned the same preference to have common comparison semantics.
This document derives the internal cost only from resolution of the path resolution tuple. The independently required BGP NEXT_HOP check contributes resolvability, not a second cost.
The MPLS case covered by is one instance of the generic mechanism defined here.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document does not require any IANA actions.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document does not define any new information exchanged between BGP speakers. Path-resolution preferences are purely local and are not advertised.

BGP attributes that contribute to a resolution key or resolution context can influence the selected path-resolution result and, consequently, BGP route selection. Existing validation and policy controls for those attributes continue to apply. Incorrect or unauthorized preference assignment or ordering can steer traffic through an unintended resolution. Assigning the same preference to results whose metrics do not have common comparison semantics can cause unlike metrics to be compared. Configuration of these local policies needs the same protection against unauthorized modification as other local routing policy.
